kagome magnet Tb6Ti4Al43

I. INTRODUCTION
Kagome lattices have attracted significant attention
in magnetic systems due to their unique geometry of
corner-sharing triangles, which naturally introduces frus-
tration in these systems [1–3]. Such materials have de-
picted many exotic, unconventional phenomena such as
flat bands due to localization of electrons in real space,
Dirac-like dispersions, strong geometric frustration, su-
perconductivity, and charge density wave [4–7]. This in-
tricate arrangement of atoms can also provide an ideal
platform for realizing the Berry curvature–driven trans-
port phenomena [8, 9]. Mn3Ge and Mn3Sn, non-collinear
antiferromagnets, in which Mn atoms form the kagome
structure, have demonstrated large anomalous Hall ef-
fects even in the absence of net magnetization, driven
by symmetry-breaking spin configurations [10, 11]. Sim-
ilarly, Fe3Sn2, which is a room temperature ferromagnet,
holds real space magnetic textures as well as Dirac cones
and flat bands in momentum space owing to the kagome
lattice frustration and anisotropy in this compound [12–
15]. Studies on AV3Sb5 (where A = K, Rb, Cs) series
also highlight the interplay of electronic topology and
correlations in kagome-based materials [16, 17].
An important characteristic of kagome material is the
presence of highly degenerate magnetic ground states
arising from geometric frustration. Consequently, these
systems are highly sensitive to perturbations such as
lattice distortions, magnetic anisotropy, and compet-
ing exchange interactions, which can lift the degener-
acy and stabilize ordered, anisotropic, or field-tunable
non-collinear magnetic states [1, 4]. For example, in
R3Ru4Al12 (R = rare earth elements), exchange inter-

actions and magnetocrystalline anisotropy partially lift
geometric frustration, allowing the system to achieve a
ground state, but show field-induced transitions [18–20].
In other systems, like HoAgGe, such distortions in the
kagome lattice modifies the band structure, leading to a
finite Berry curvature, resulting in an enhanced anoma-
lous Hall effect [21].
A similar system is Tb6Ti4Al43, which hosts a distorted
kagome lattice formed by magnetic Tb3+ ions. The sys-
tem retains key ingredients such as geometric frustra-
tion, strong magnetocrystalline anisotropy, and compet-
ing magnetic interactions. The magnetic properties of
the broader R6T4Al43 family, where R = rare-earth el-
ements and T = Ti, V, Nb, Ta, Cr, Mo, W have been
previously investigated by Wolff et al. in polycrystalline
samples, where metamagnetic transitions were reported
in several compounds [22, 23]. In addition, single crystal
growth of this family and studies on Dy6Cr4Al43 reveal
a strong magnetic anisotropy, indicating the importance
of anisotropic effects in this family [24, 25].
Here, we present a comprehensive investigation of the
magnetic, electrical, and specific heat properties of the
single crystal of Tb6Ti4Al43 to uncover the interplay be-
tween anisotropic magnetism, field-induced spin reorien-
tation, and the charge-carrier response. It exhibits pro-
nounced magnetic anisotropy and field-induced metam-
agnetic transitions, indicating the presence of compet-
ing magnetic ground states. Despite its antiferromag-
netic (AFM) ground state ordering with TN ∼ 19 K, the
system exhibits a clear anomalous Hall effect, which we
attribute to a field-induced spin-polarized state emerg-
ing through low-field metamagnetic transitions for H ∥
c. A significant intrinsic contribution to the anomalous

ture induced effects due to the momentum space topol-

netic anisotropy, evidenced by its anisotropic magnetic
response along different crystal directions and the ten-
dency to physically reorient itself along the magnetic easy
axis (c axis).
II. EXPERIMENTAL DETAILS
Single crystals of Tb6Ti4Al43 were grown using the
flux method. High purity elements Tb (99.99 %), Ti
powder (Alfa Aesar, 99.99 %), and Al (99.99 %) were
mixed in an optimized ratio of 40:3:1000 to obtain single
phase Tb6Ti4Al43 single crystals. All the elements
were handled in an argon-filled glove box because Tb
is air-sensitive. The total mass of 3 g was placed in
an alumina crucible, which was then vacuum sealed in
a quartz tube. The sealed ampoule was first heated
to 1000 °C at the rate of 100 °C/h and held at this
temperature for 24 hours to ensure a homogeneous
solution. It was then slowly cooled to 750 °C at the
rate of 2 °C/h. At this temperature, the ampoule was
centrifuged to separate the crystals from the excess
aluminium flux. The resulting crystals were silvery, with
a hexagonal cross-section, and approximately 1-2 mm in
size (shown in the insets of Figs. 1(c) and 1(d)).
The elemental composition of the crystal was analyzed
using the Energy Dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS)
with Hitachi High-Technol TM 3000 with 15 keV energy.
The measured elemental composition of Tb, Ti, and
Al was found close to the stoichiometric ratio of 6:4:43
within the experimental uncertainty. The orientation of
the crystal was confirmed using the Proto x-ray Laue
diffraction with white x-rays. The θ - 2θ x-ray diffrac-
tion measurements were carried out using the HR-XRD
(PANalytical Empyrean X-Ray diffractometer) with a
Cu Kα (λ = 1.5406 ˚A) monochromatic source at room
temperature. Magnetic measurements, including both
in-plane and out-of-plane dc and ac magnetization, were
performed using the commercial 7 T Quantum Design
Magnetic Property Measurement System (MPMS-3). A
quartz sample holder was used to measure the magneti-
zation along the c-axis, while a brass holder was used
for measurements along the hard axis of the crystal.
Electrical transport and specific heat measurements
were performed using the commercial Quantum Design
Physical Property Measurement System (PPMS). For
resistivity measurements, a standard linear four-probe
geometry was employed, using platinum wire and silver
paint for electrical contacts.

Temperature-dependent magnetization measured under
an applied field of 500 Oe along and perpendicular to the
crystallographic c - direction in the temperature range
2 K - 50 K is depicted in Fig. 2(c). A clear magnetic

TN , suggesting the presence of weak uncompensated mo-

Further, to understand the effect of long-range mag-

temperature-dependent zero-field resistivity measure-

due to the reduction of spin-disorder scattering as the
long-range AFM ordering is established in the system.

To probe the effect of magnetic field on the material,
we performed isothermal field-dependent magnetization
measurements, M (H ), for the magnetic field applied
along the c-axis and within the ab-plane of the crystal.
For H ∥ c at 2 K, a strongly asymmetric magnetization
response is observed, as shown in Fig. 4(a). The magneti-
zation initially increases gradually with field as expected
from the AFM ground state, but around 1 T, a strong
metamagnetic transition occurs which aligns moments to
a saturated state (marked as curve 1). Upon decreasing
the field, the magnetization remains almost constant, re-
taining a remanent value comparable to the saturation
magnetization, and collapses to nearly zero upon appli-
cation of a small reverse field (marked as curve 2). The
same process is reproduced in the negative field cycle,
where a sharp metamagnetic switching occurs near -1 T.
Notably, the envelope hysteresis loop lies inside the vir-
gin magnetization curve (curve 4), indicating pronounced
magnetic hysteresis and irreversible field-dependent be-
haviour. Such a behaviour is commonly associated with
metastability and phase coexistence during field-induced
magnetic transitions [30–32]. Fig. 4(b) shows the M (H )
curves measured at 3 K and 5 K. With increasing tem-
perature, the virgin curve progressively approaches the
hysteresis loop, accompanied by a noticeable reduction
in the hysteresis area, suggesting a weakening of the irre-
versible metamagnetic behaviour due to thermal effects.
M (H ) curves at higher temperatures are depicted in Fig.
4(c), where the metamagnetic transitions are reversible.
Next, we measured field-dependent magnetization
(M (H )) with the magnetic field applied perpendicular
to the c-axis of the crystal (H ⊥ c). The crystal was
mounted on the brass sample holder, where it was firmly
clamped between two small quartz rods to prevent any
mechanical movement. The (M (H )) curves depicted in
Fig. 4(d) reveal irreversible spin-flop–like transitions at
2 K and 3 K, which becomes reversible at higher tem-
peratures. Even at the highest applied field of 7 T, the
FIG. 5. (a) Temperature-dependent ZFC and FCW magnetization at different magnetic fields for H ∥ c, (b) temperature-
dependent specific heat at different magnetic fields for H ∥ c.
magnetization does not reach saturation. This behaviour
suggests a strong magnetocrystalline anisotropy in the
system, where the c-axis acts as an easy axis for the
crystal. When the magnetic field is applied along the
hard axis, the system undergoes a field-induced spin re-
orientation rather than complete alignment of magnetic
moments with the field, leading to spin-flop transitions
and the absence of full saturation within the measured
field range.
Notably, care must be taken when mounting this crystal
for measurements with the magnetic field applied along
the hard axis of the crystal. Fig. S1 (see supplemen-
tary material) provides the cases of field-induced crystal
reorientation observed when the field is applied within
the ab plane of the crystal (H ⊥ c) [33]. During mag-
netic and electrical measurements for H ⊥ c, it was re-
peatedly observed that the crystal physically rotated on
the sample holder, with its orientation changing so that
the applied field aligned approximately along the crys-
tal’s easy axis. This suggests the presence of magnetic
torque acting on the crystal, possibly due to the compe-
tition between the Zeeman energy and the magnetocrys-
talline anisotropy energy. When the magnetic torque be-
comes sufficiently large to overcome the mechanical con-
straint imposed by the mounting medium, the crystal
undergoes field-induced physical reorientation. To ob-
tain quantitative insights into the strength and nature of
the anisotropy, torque magnetometry measurements on
this crystal will be extremely useful.
To further investigate the effect of the magnetic field
on the magnetic transitions in this distorted kagome lat-
tice, we performed temperature-dependent magnetiza-
tion M(T) measurements under zero-field-cooled (ZFC)
and field-cooled warming (FCW) conditions at various
applied fields (shown in Fig. 5(a)). The M (T) curves
exhibit a clear peak corresponding to the AFM order-
ing temperature. For fields up to 0.3 T, the ZFC and
FCW curves overlap, indicating reversibility of the AFM
behaviour. However, there is also a weak kink-like fea-
ture indicating the presence of a field-induced magnetic
phase near the AFM ordering temperature. As the mag-
netic field increases to 0.5 T, a bifurcation between the
ZFC and FCW curves emerges below 10 K, indicating
field-induced changes in the spin configuration. At 0.7
T, a sharp step-like increase in M(T) emerges at T < 10
K, coinciding with the region of field-induced metamag-
netic transition. This behaviour suggests an irreversible
magnetic state where Zeeman energy effectively competes
with the exchange interactions, driving a transition from
the compensated AFM state to a canted or field-polarized
state. In this regime, the system exhibits signatures of
both AFM ordering and a ferromagnetic-like contribu-
tion at low temperatures. With a further increase in the
magnetic field, the peak corresponding to the AFM or-
der progressively weakens, indicating suppression of the
magnetic ground state. The system evolves toward a
strongly canted or field-polarized magnetic state, accom-
panied by a pronounced bifurcation between the ZFC
and FCW curves. Above 1 T, the magnetization shows
a smooth temperature dependence without a distinct
transition feature, consistent with a field-polarized mag-
netic state. The behaviour is further verified by the
temperature-dependent specific heat measurements con-
ducted at different magnetic fields, as illustrated in Fig.
5(b). As the field increases, the peak corresponding to
the transition to long-range AFM ordering shifts to lower
temperatures and decreases in intensity, indicating sup-
pression of the ground-state magnetic interaction as the
system approaches the field-induced spin-saturated state.

To gain more insight into the field-induced magnetic
state just below TN , we performed frequency-dependent
ac susceptibility measurements under an applied dc mag-
netic field of 3000 Oe. The ac susceptibility shows a
systematic decrease in peak intensity as frequency in-
creases, accompanied by a discernible shift in the peak
temperature. The shift is more clearly observed in the
imaginary part of the ac susceptibility. This behaviour
is expected in relaxing systems; as the frequency de-
creases, the magnetic spins have more time to follow the
ac drive, leading to increased response in the intensity.
The frequency-dependent shift in the peak suggests the
presence of slow-relaxation dynamics in the system, pos-
sibly glassy behaviour. The spin relaxation time in the
system is then evaluated using the critical slowing down
(CSD) model, given by : τ = τ0 (Tf /Tg − 1)−zν, where
τ is inverse of the applied frequency (f ), Tf is the spin
freezing temperature at a particular frequency f, Tg is the
spin freezing temperature at f → 0, zν is dynamical crit-
ical constant, and τ0 is the microscopic spin flipping time
[34–37]. The fitting of curve between τ and Tf according
to CSD model yields Tg as depicted in Fig. 6(g). The
derived Tg is then used to plot log10f vs log10(Tf /Tg
- 1), the linear fit is used to calculate the spin relax-
ation time, τo and the critical constant, presented in Fig.
6(h). The antilog of the curve intercept (shown in Fig.
6h) corresponds to the spin relaxation time τ0 ∼ 4.82 ×
10−9 s. The nanosecond-scale relaxation time is consis-
tent with the slow collective magnetic dynamics in the
system. This supports the possibility of cluster-like dy-
namics under the applied field, in close proximity to the
AFM transition.
To understand the effect of the field-induced magnetic
state on the conduction charge carriers, we performed
isothermal field-dependent resistivity measurements, as
presented in Fig. 7. The longitudinal resistivity, ρzz,
measured with I ∥ V ∥ H ∥ z, is presented in Figs.
7(a) - 7(d). At 2 K [Fig. 7(a)], the resistivity shows
a weak field-dependence at low fields (indicated as 1),
corresponding to the AFM ground state where the mag-
netization increases approximately linearly with the field.
A sharp drop in resistivity is observed at the metamag-
netic transition, which marks the field-induced transition

from the AFM to spin-polarized state. The suppression
of spin-disorder scattering due to the alignment of mo-
ments results in a lower resistive state. At higher fields,
the resistivity gradually increases, giving rise to positive
magnetoresistivity. During the subsequent field sweep
from +9 T to 0 T, the resistivity decreases smoothly with-
out exhibiting any additional anomaly (marked as 2), in-
dicating spin-polarized state that persists over this field
range, consistent with the hysteretic magnetization be-
haviour shown in Fig. 4(a). Upon further field sweep to-
wards the negative field, a clear peak is observed (marked
as 3), corresponding to the metamagnetic jump in the
negative cycle. This peak can be attributed to enhanced
magnetic disorder, which increases the electron scatter-
ing. Upon increasing the negative magnetic field be-
yond the transition, the resistivity increases again on the
negative side, reflecting the re-establishment of a neg-
atively spin-polarized state with reduced spin-disorder
scattering. Overall, the field-dependence of the resistiv-
ity closely follows the magnetic phase evolution, demon-
strating a strong interplay between the Tb3+ 4f moments
and conduction electrons. Figs. 7(b) and 7(c) show the
ρzz(H) at 3 K and 5 K, respectively. The overall be-
haviour is similar to that observed at 2K. However, the
intensity of the resistive peak at the metamagnetic tran-
sition increases with the temperature. This enhancement
is consistent with the increased spin-disorder scattering
arising from thermal fluctuations. The ρzz(H) behaviour
at higher temperatures is depicted in Fig. 7(d), where a
similar trend is observed. Although the positive mag-
netoresistance corresponding to the spin-polarized state
is retained, the sharp resistivity peaks are indistinguish-
able due to the disappearance of magnetic hysteresis in
the magnetization measurements.
The transverse magnetoresistivity, measured with H ∥ z
and I ∥ V ∥ x is presented in Figs. 7(e) - 7(h). The
overall resistivity behaviour is qualitatively similar to the
longitudinal configuration, confirming that the transport
anomalies originate from the same field-induced magnetic
transitions. Compared to the longitudinal geometry,
the peak anomalies are considerably more pronounced
in this configuration, indicating that the in-plane mag-
netic transport is more sensitive to the reorientation of
the Tb moments. Attempts were also made to measure
the resistivity with magnetic field applied in the ab plane.
However, reliable measurements could not be performed
in that configuration as the sample exhibited a tendency
of rotation, eventually leading to the failure of electrical
contacts.
To further investigate the influence of magnetic states
on the charge carriers, Hall measurements were per-
formed. The field-dependent Hall resistivity (ρyx(H))
of Tb6Ti4Al43 was measured at various temperatures
with H ∥ z, V ∥ y, and I ∥ x, as depicted in Fig.
8. At low temperatures, the ρyx(H) (Fig. 8(a)) shows
an irreversible Hall response, closely following the hys-
teretic magnetization behaviour associated with the field-
induced metamagnetic transition. During the initial field
sweep, the Hall resistivity changes abruptly across the
metamagnetic transition and subsequently becomes re-
versible once the system enters the field-polarized state.

Therefore, the Hall resistivity data are presented in their
measured form at low temperatures in Figs. 8(a) and
8(b). In the high field region, where the Hall signal is
reversible, the antisymmetrization procedure can be em-
ployed to minimize the effects due to the longitudinal re-
sistivity component that might be contributing due to the
slight voltage-contact misalignment. Fig 8(c) presents
the antisymmetrized ρyx(H) from 7 K to 20 K. The cor-
responding Hall conductivity is obtained using σyx = -
ρyx/(ρ2yx+ρ2xx). For 2 K - 5 K, the antisymmetrized Hall
data in the reversible region above 2 T are utilized to
obtain the σyx as shown in Fig. 8(d). For temperatures
7 K - 25 K, the resulting Hall conductivity in the entire
field range, σyx, is presented in Fig. 8(e).
The experimentally measured ρyx(H) can be expressed
as the sum of the ordinary Hall effect (OHE) and the
anomalous Hall effect (AHE),
ρyx = R0µ0H + RsM (6)
where R0 is the ordinary Hall coefficient, Rs is the anoma-
lous Hall coefficient, and M is the isothermal magneti-
zation [9, 38, 39]. The experimental and fitted curves at
7 K are presented in Fig. 8(f), indicating the magnetic
origin of the anomalous Hall effect in Tb6Ti4Al43.
Fig. 8(g) depicts the anomalous Hall conductivity
(AHC), which is derived by subtracting the ordinary Hall
contribution, determined from the linear fit of the high-
field region of the σyx(H) (Figs. 8(d) and 8(e)) from
the total Hall conductivity. At 2 K, the AHC (σyAx)
reaches 500 S cm−1, and gradually decreases in magni-
tude with increasing temperature, following the suppres-
sion of magnetic field-induced transitions. To distinguish
the different contributions to the AHE, the scaling rela-
tion was employed [38–40].
ρAyx = Aρxx + Bρ2xx (7)
Here, the linear term, Aρxx, is associated with the
extrinsic skew scattering mechanism, whereas the
quadratic term, Bρ2xx, contains contributions from both
the intrinsic Berry curvature and the extrinsic side-jump
mechanism. Fig. 8(h) presents the plot of ρAyx/ρxx
versus ρxx, from which the coefficients A and B are
obtained by fitting to the scaling relation (7). The
corresponding temperature dependence of AHC arising
from the skew scattering and the quadratic (intrinsic
+ side jump) contributions is shown in Fig. 8(i). The
quadratic contribution reaches a magnitude of ≈ 2000
S cm−1, indicating a substantial contribution from
the intrinsic and side jump mechanism. The scaling
relation cannot separate the contributions from each
of the mechanisms. The possible magnitude of the
side jump mechanism can be theoretically estimated
using σysjx ∼ (e2/ha)(ϵso/EF ), where a is the lattice
constant, ϵso is the spin-orbit interaction energy, and
EF is the Fermi energy. For a conventional metallic
system, (ϵso/EF ) is of the order of 10−2 or smaller,
and hence the estimated side jump for Tb6Ti4Al43
contributes around ∼ 3.5 S cm−1 for a ∼ 11 ˚A[40–43].
This is substantially smaller than the experimentally
obtained quadratic contribution magnitude of ∼ 2000
S cm−1. The large quadratic contribution is therefore
consistent with an intrinsic mechanism generated by the
topological band structure. In contrast, the contribution
of skew scattering reaches ≈ 2500 S cm−1. The skew-
scattering and quadratic contributions have opposite
signs and largely compensate each other, resulting in a
net anomalous Hall conductivity of approximately 500 S
cm−1. Although skew scattering constitutes an extrinsic
contribution, the large contribution due to the intrinsic
AHC is particularly interesting, as it reflects the Berry
curvature of the occupied electronic states and may be
associated with the underlying electronic band structure
IV. CONCLUSION
In summary, we have synthesized single crystals of
the distorted kagome compound Tb6Ti4Al43 and demon-
[1] L. Balents, Spin liquids in frustrated magnets, Nature
strated the coupling of its electrical, magnetic and ther-
modynamic responses. The material orders antiferro-
magnetically around 19 K and shows pronounced mag-
netic anisotropy, likely due to the distorted Tb kagome
magnetic layer. For H ∥ c, a sharp field-induced meta-
magnetic transition at an applied field of 1 T, switches
the system from the AFM to a spin-polarized state which
collapses upon application of a small negative field. This
is reminiscent of the unequal write and erase fields used
in magnetic switching. For a field applied along the
hard axis, the crystal exhibits spin-flop behaviour and
a tendency to rotate towards the easy axis. The field-
induced magnetic transitions are also reflected in the elec-
trical transport measurements. Both longitudinal and
transverse resistivity follow the magnetization, leading
to jumps at the metamagnetic switching. This shows the
strong coupling between the 4f electrons and the con-
duction carriers in the system, giving a direct electri-
cal readout of the magnetic state. Despite being AFM,
the anomalous Hall contribution of 500 S cm−1 is ob-
served corresponding to the field-induced transitions. A
large contribution to AHC arises due to the intrinsic
mechanisms, suggesting the presence of topological elec-
tronic band structure. The combination of strong mag-
netic anisotropy, field-controlled switching between the
AFM and spin-polarized states, field-induced mechan-
ical reorientation, and intrinsic anomalous Hall contri-
bution demonstrates the interplay between spin, charge,
and topology in Tb6Ti4Al43. This work suggests that
the distorted kagome R6T4Al43 family can provide a fer-
tile platform for exploring electrically readable magnetic
switching, spin manipulation, and magneto-mechanical
functionalities.
